evidence: Traffic — the request rate the system must sustain, expressed in requests per second (rps) or queries per second, plus concurrency levels and burstiness.
issue: Three-way definitional contradiction about whether concurrency is a workload input. Ch 4 §4.1.1 p.57 lists 'concurrency levels' under the Traffic (workload) dimension; the Preface p.13 operational checklist also lists 'concurrency' under 'What is the workload?'; but Ch 6 §6.1.1 p.111 states flatly 'Concurrency is not a workload input: it is a serving-side quantity derived from the arrival rate and the time in system (Little's law), so it belongs with queue depth on the scheduler side, not in this layer.' Fig 6.1 p.113 then labels the workload box 'rps · token profile · concurrency', and the caption tries to reinterpret the entry as λ.
fix_instruction: Pick one classification and apply it everywhere. Recommended: treat concurrency as a derived serving-side quantity (Ch 6's position), and rewrite Ch 4 §4.1.1 and the Preface p.13 checklist to say 'traffic (rps) and burstiness', moving concurrency out of the workload dimension. Then remove the 'concurrency' entry from Fig 6.1's workload box (or relabel it 'request rate λ').

evidence: The canonical workload is prefill-FLOP- and KV-capacity-dominated, but decode-latency-dominated because of that long context, not because of the ratio — three distinct senses of 'dominated' (share of FLOPs, capacity pressure, share of wall-clock), and the third does not contradict the first two
issue: Prose clarity / semantic overload: the sentence uses 'dominated' three times in one sentence with three different meanings (share of FLOPs, capacity pressure, share of wall-clock) and then apologizes for the overload in a parenthetical rather than fixing the wording. A reader skimming this can misread the canonical workload as decode-bound in the resource sense.
fix_instruction: Replace the overloaded word with three distinct verbs, e.g.: 'The canonical workload's FLOP share is prefill-heavy and its capacity pressure is KV-heavy, but its per-request wall-clock is decode-heavy because of the long output, not because of the input/output ratio — the three are different senses of load and none contradicts the others.'

evidence: 1.29 PFLOP / ~1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS demand > 0.989 PFLOPS H100 peak; with the attention term included (~1.51 PFLOP) the demand is ~1.40 PFLOPS
issue: Units inconsistency inside one table cell. The first sentence uses the noun 'PFLOP' for the work quantity (1.29 PFLOP) and 'PFLOPS' for the rate (1.19 PFLOPS) — correct — but the phrase '~1.51 PFLOP' is then described as the attention-included 'demand', and the next clause converts it to '1.40 PFLOPS'. The same numeric quantity is written with two different unit suffixes (PFLOP vs PFLOPS) in one sentence, and the second value (1.40) is a rate, not a work quantity, which is easy to misread as a second work figure.
fix_instruction: Split the cell into two clauses with explicit unit labels: '1.29 PFLOP (work) / ~1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS (rate) > 0.989 PFLOPS H100 peak. Adding the attention term gives ~1.51 PFLOP of work, i.e. ~1.40 PFLOPS of required rate.' Never write 'the demand is ~1.51 PFLOP' — a demand is a rate, so it should always be PFLOPS.
